The two discharges compared were #79423 with a carbon wall and #81928 with the ITER-like wall (ILW).
In the carbon wall case (#79423), a runaway electron plateau of 600 kA was observed, while in the ILW case (#81928), the runaway current was negligibly small (less than 70 kA).
The pre-disruption plasma current was around 1.9 MA, the magnetic field was 2 T, the elongation was 1.3, and the effective charge (Zeff) was around 2.2-2.5.
The total number of injected argon atoms was 7.39x10^20 for #79423, 30% higher than the 5.68x10^20 amount for #81928.
The thermal quench occurred at slightly different times with respect to the argon valve trigger, with a 30 ms difference between the two discharges.
In the ILW case (#81928), the temperature dropped down to 300 eV due to the low radiation intensity and slower transport times during the current quench.
The authors used a one-dimensional model that solves coupled differential equations for the runaway density, heat diffusion, and plasma current in the presence of impurity injection.
The model includes Dreicer generation, runaway avalanching, and losses due to radial diffusion from magnetic perturbations.
The authors performed scans of the argon and background impurity (carbon or beryllium) contents to investigate their effects on runaway electron generation.
The results indicate that the differences in runaway electron generation between the carbon wall and ILW cases are greatly reduced above 50% argon content.

The authors found that the reason for the changed runaway electron dynamics is a complex, combined effect of differences in plasma parameter profiles, radiation characteristics, and injected argon amount.
The authors assessed the effect of magnetic perturbations on runaway electron suppression, but did not provide the specific level of perturbation required.
The authors note that the reliability of Zeff measurements during the disruption is low, and values during and after the thermal quench have to be considered with caution.
The authors state that the ionization/recombination and radiation calculation is the most CPU-intensive task in the numerical model.
The authors found that the change in plasma electron density with the experimentally measured magnitude of 30% has a negligible effect on the saturation runaway current.
